cells.tense: Imagining forward is happening now, out in the open, and you are holding the pen while it runs.
cells.act: keep the motivation warm with steady care
cells.ask: Pick one bond you want to keep growing and give it a single small act of care — a call, a shared hour, a note — small enough that you could do it worn out.
cells.core:
You can imagine what a closeness might become and stay with it while it takes shape. Where two people meet, you sense the shape of what's possible between you before there's evidence for it, and you don't rush it into a verdict. That isn't naivety. It's how you find the real thing early, while it's still soft enough to shape.

The risk in that is drift: the imagining stays warm and the thing itself doesn't get watered. Pick one bond you want to keep growing and give it a single small act of care — a call, a shared hour, a note. Small enough that you could do it worn out. You'll learn quickly whether what you sensed is there, and you'll have moved instead of only seen.

cells.tense: The imagining is running ahead into a future you can't write in, and it is bracing before anyone gets there.
cells.act: tend the small thing and learn from it
cells.ask: Take one relationship you're bracing about and tend one small concrete thing inside it — show up, listen, do the unglamorous task — and let what it needs teach you.
cells.core:
Where two people meet, you're already several scenes ahead. You can see how the closeness goes, where it frays, what it costs — and you're bracing for a version of it that hasn't arrived. It reads as care. From the other side, it can feel like being managed before anything has happened.

Care has a slower half: staying with the thing as it is and doing the work it currently needs. Take one relationship you're bracing about and tend one small concrete thing in it — show up, listen, do the unglamorous task. Let that teach you what's actually there. It won't settle the bracing, but it gives you real material to replace the imagined version with, a piece at a time.

cells.tense: The imagining stopped some time back, and you are standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.act: ask the question you do not know the answer to
cells.ask: Ask someone a real question you don't know the answer to — how they actually are — and stay quiet through the whole answer without steering it anywhere.
cells.core:
Where two people meet, you're not reaching for the possible version anymore. You've learned what to expect and you're holding that instead, answering from the known place before the live thing gets a chance to speak. The warmth is there. The reach isn't.

What that needs is not more feeling — it's more knowing. Ask one person a real question you don't know the answer to, how they actually are, and stay quiet through the whole reply without steering it. There may be more going on than you had written down. One question won't refill everything, but it puts you back at a door you can actually walk through, and it gives you something true to stand on before you decide what you feel about it.

cells.tense: You are already doing the imagining and the reaching, and someone else's name is on it in your own account.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Write three moments from the last month when someone moved toward you — plain order, names and events only, no feelings attached — and read it once without arguing it down.
cells.core:
You're reading the room well — catching what's shifting in people, saying the timely thing, moving toward them before they ask. And you'd describe yourself as just being around. The instinct is real and it's yours; you've filed it under circumstance, or under the other person's warmth, so it doesn't get counted as something you did.

Before filing it under luck, get it in writing. Take three moments from the last month when someone actually moved toward you and write them down in plain order — names and events, no feelings. Read it once without arguing it down. A thing you can read without feeling words is a thing you can stop attributing to chance. What you do with that is yours; you don't owe it a label.

attempts.check: The one unsupported claim is that the person's feeling-with is currently landing as connection repeatedly enough that others lean on it — the record supports the capacity, not its reception. A reader could reasonably say the alignment only happens with certain people, or that they've stopped reaching at all; the Too Little core leans on that second reading and hedges it with a door already behind them. The asks survive being wrong: each is a small, self-contained act of imagining, tending, listening, or writing, useful whether or not the status is right. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'and the people you're with feel it land' — cut; it praised a method instead of describing. Cells written with that removed.
